To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
air pollution is a significant risk factor for adverse maternal and infant health outcomes, that air pollution exposure disparities exist in the US and that these disparities are not well understood.
the use of a spatially varying coefficient model is a useful tool in air pollution research to identify exposure disparities.

1) the spatial distribution of air pollution is not uniform and varies across space and time; 2) vulnerable populations are more likely than the general population to be exposed to higher air pollution concentrations and to be exposed to air pollutants at higher levels than the general population; 3) vulnerable populations are also more likely to live near sources of air pollution; 4) the spatial distribution and temporal trends of air pollution are related to the spatial distribution of vulnerable populations and their exposures to air pollutants;
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (i) identifying and quantifying the impact of differential exposures in air pollution epidemiological studies, (ii) developing and testing methods for identifying exposure disparities in air pollutant monitoring networks, (iii) evaluating the potential impact of exposure disparities on air pollution epidemiological study results, and (iv) evaluating the impact of exposure disparities in air pollutants on health disparities in vulnerable populations.
the development of methods to identify and quantify exposure disparities in air pollutants and their impact on health.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is an association between maternal air pollution exposure and adverse birth outcomes.
there are many methodological approaches that can be taken in the study of health disparities in air pollution and health, but there are no clear-cut approaches that can be used in every study.
the evidence for the association of air pollution with adverse birth outcomes is mixed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of a spatially explicit air pollution model is necessary to identify exposure disparities and their impacts on adverse birth outcomes.
air pollutants have a negative impact on maternal and infant health, and these effects are worse for minority populations and those with lower income and education.
we have identified a method to identify exposure disparities in air pollutant epidemiology specific to preterm birth.
The main takeaway from our work is that

air pollution is not distributed evenly across the population and the spatial distribution of pollutant levels is not random; therefore, it is important to consider the spatial distribution when assessing the relationship between air pollutant levels and health outcomes.

air pollutant exposure estimates should be tailored to the study population and health outcome of interest, and that air pollutant exposures are not homogenous in a geographic region, even in a small region like New York City.

the use of pollutant monitors located in areas of higher pollution levels and higher density of pollutants sources may lead to biased estimates of the association between air pollution and adverse birth outcomes, especially in vulnerable populations.
